item.title: VASSPR: starting vasopressin at 0.1 instead of 0.4 mcg/kg/min of norepinephrine does not lower septic shock mortality
item.description:
JAMA · RCT · 2026-10-14

A 13-hospital cluster-crossover trial in Utah and Idaho (3,959 patients) compared hospital policies of adding fixed-dose vasopressin at 0.1 vs 0.4 mcg/kg/min norepinephrine-equivalent.

Take-home

  • 28-day mortality 31.8% vs 33.0%; adjusted OR 0.98. Vasopressin use 52% vs 33%.
  • No gain in kidney replacement-free, vasopressor-free or ICU-free days.
  • Exploratory signal of more cardiogenic shock with early vasopressin (7.4% vs 6.3%).

Why it matters. Observational data and a reinforcement-learning analysis (OVISS, JAMA 2025) suggested that adding vasopressin earlier, at low norepinephrine doses, might save lives. VASSPR, presented at ESICM LIVES 2026 and published in JAMA on 14 October 2026, is the first randomized test of a threshold strategy at scale.

What they did. Peltan and colleagues ran a pragmatic cluster-randomized, cluster-crossover trial across 13 Intermountain Health hospitals, which switched monthly between a policy of starting vasopressin 0.03 units/min when norepinephrine-equivalent reached 0.1 mcg/kg/min and a policy of starting it at 0.4 mcg/kg/min. 3,959 adults with septic shock were included between February 2024 and July 2025. The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality.

What they found. Vasopressin was given to 52.4% of patients under the lower threshold vs 32.9% under the higher one. Mortality at 28 days was 31.8% (628/1,975) vs 33.0% (655/1,984); adjusted OR 0.98 (95% CI 0.87-1.06), adjusted risk difference -0.4 points (95% CI -2.7 to 1.3). Kidney replacement therapy-free days, vasopressor-free days, ICU-free days, 90-day and in-hospital mortality were all unchanged. Arrhythmia (18.4% vs 18.1%) and soft-tissue ischemia (0.8% vs 0.7%) did not differ; persistent or new cardiogenic shock was 7.4% vs 6.3% (adjusted OR 1.19), an exploratory finding.

Caveats. Open label, policy-level randomization with incomplete adherence (45% strict adherence to the lower threshold), and the trial excludes a large benefit rather than proving equivalence.

For anesthesiologists. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign says add vasopressin when norepinephrine is escalating without a number; VASSPR says there is no mortality reason to rush it at 0.1. In the cardiac ICU, where vasopressin is often favored for vasoplegia and pulmonary vascular reasons, the choice stays physiological rather than threshold-driven.

item.title: Across 31 European countries, 15% of cesareans get general anesthesia, and 54% when it is a true emergency
item.description:
BJA · Observational · 2026-10-09

Prospective cohort of 9,989 cesarean deliveries at 361 European centres (Sept 2023 to Apr 2025), recording anaesthetic technique and reasons for GA by urgency category.

Take-home

  • GA overall 14.8%: emergency 54%, urgent 14%, expedited 11%, elective 11%.
  • Neuraxial-to-GA conversion 7.7% overall, 23% in emergencies, still 6% in elective cases.
  • Maternal request drove nearly half of elective GAs; lack of time drove most emergency GAs.

Why it matters. General anaesthesia for cesarean carries higher maternal risk and more neonatal depression, and GA rates are a core obstetric anaesthesia quality indicator. Contemporary, prospective, multinational data have been missing.

What they did. A prospective cohort enrolled every cesarean delivery, with no exclusions, at 361 centres in 31 European countries between 1 September 2023 and 30 April 2025. Anaesthetists recorded technique and urgency on a four-level scale (emergency, urgent, expedited, elective) and the reason for GA.

What they found. Among 9,989 cesarean deliveries, 14.8% (95% CI 14.0-15.5) involved general anaesthesia. By urgency: emergency 54.0%, urgent 13.8%, expedited 11.3%, elective 10.9%. GA was the planned first technique in 7.6%; in elective cases maternal request was the leading reason (47%), while in emergencies insufficient time for neuraxial dominated (58%). Conversion from a neuraxial technique to GA occurred in 7.7% of 9,228 cases: 23.1% in emergencies but still 6.1% in elective cases.

Caveats. Observational, with centre-level variation the design cannot explain, and participation was voluntary, so the sample may skew toward engaged departments. Maternal and neonatal outcomes were not the primary focus.

For the anesthesiologist. Two numbers deserve a look in your own unit: an elective conversion rate of 6% suggests many spinals are coming up short, and an elective GA-on-request rate near 5% suggests counselling and anxiolysis pathways are underused. Read alongside the MID-CD pain data: inadequate neuraxial blocks, not just emergencies, drive GA exposure.

item.title: EUROMACS: HeartMate 3 recipients under 50 have 75% five-year on-device survival, close to transplant-list figures
item.description:
Eur J Cardiothorac Surg · Registry · 2026-10-07

The European MCS registry reports five-year outcomes in 2,850 HeartMate 3 recipients by age; the youngest group survives on device at rates the authors compare with transplant listing, reopening the LVAD-first debate.

Take-home

  • Five-year on-device survival: 74.7% under 50, 65.5% at 50 to 59, 53.9% at 60 to 69, 48.8% at 70 plus.
  • Recovery explant 4.3% in the youngest group versus 0.4% in the oldest.
  • Stroke, infection and malfunction were similar across ages; bleeding was lower in the young.

Why it matters. The LVAD-versus-transplant question is sharpest in young patients, who have the most years to gain or lose. EUROMACS, the European MCS registry, has now followed enough HeartMate 3 recipients to report five-year results by age (Gallone and colleagues, Turin; Eur J Cardiothorac Surg, accepted manuscript online 7 October 2026).

What they did. 2,850 adults with HeartMate 3 in EUROMACS, grouped as under 50 (23.5%), 50 to 59 (29.7%), 60 to 69 (38.0%) and 70 or older (8.8%). Primary outcome was five-year on-device survival, censored at transplant or explant; a competing-risk analysis was added.

What they found.

  • On-device survival at five years: 74.7% under 50, 65.5% at 50 to 59, 53.9% at 60 to 69, 48.8% at 70 or older.
  • Explant for myocardial recovery: 4.3% in the youngest group versus 0.4% in the oldest.
  • With transplant as a competing risk, five-year cumulative death was 20.8% in the youngest group and 49.5% in the oldest, with higher transplant rates in the young driving much of the gap.
  • Bleeding-free survival was better in younger patients; stroke, device infection and malfunction were similar across ages.

The authors' point. Patients under 50 on a HeartMate 3 have five-year survival close to what is reported for patients listed for transplant, so prolonged LVAD support before transplant deserves study as a way to maximize lifetime benefit in selected, motivated candidates.

Caveats. Registry data; selection into LVAD versus direct listing is not random, and censoring at transplant flatters the device in the group most likely to be transplanted.

For us. A young HeartMate 3 patient is a long-term patient. Plan for years of non-cardiac surgery, pregnancy questions and driveline management rather than months of bridging.

item.title: FDA Class I recall of every Automated Impella Controller: purge-sensor failures tied to 37 injuries and 3 deaths
item.description:
FDA · Safety alert · 2026-09-24

The FDA classified Abiomed's worldwide correction of Automated Impella Controllers as Class I after purge-flag failures stopped controllers recognizing a seated purge cassette, capping a year with three Class I Impella recalls all tied to the purge system.

Take-home

  • All AICs are in scope; use them until Abiomed fixes the purge flag; reseat the disc, then swap controllers if alarms persist.
  • Earlier 2026 Class I recalls: Generation 1 purge cassettes (Impella RP sets) and seven Impella CP SmartAssist sets.
  • Clean controller housings only with mild detergent; keep a backup controller for OR cases and transports.

Why it matters. Impella is now standard of care in STEMI shock, and 2026 brought three Class I (most serious) FDA recalls plus a Class I introducer recall, all tied to the purge system or its sensing. If you run or receive these pumps, the alarms and workarounds matter.

The recalls.

  • Automated Impella Controller (AIC), all units worldwide. Early Alert 3 September 2026, Class I notice updated 24 September. The purge flag in the purge pressure sensor assembly can fail, so the controller may not recognize that the purge cassette is seated. As of 17 August: 37 serious injuries and 3 deaths. Controllers can stay in use until Abiomed replaces the purge flag and retainer. If a purge alarm appears, reseat the purge disc; if it persists, switch to a backup AIC. Clean the housing with mild detergent only, since improper cleaning damages the flag.
  • Impella CP Set with SmartAssist, seven serial numbers (Class I, 2 July 2026): units out of specification causing low purge pressure from the start of a case with possible loss of support; three pump exchanges and one death reported.
  • Generation 1 purge cassettes, including those in Impella RP sets (Class I, 3 April 2026): purge leaks leading to low purge pressure, biomaterial ingress and unexpected pump stop; four serious injuries. Move to Generation 2 cassettes.
  • 14 Fr and 23 Fr introducer kits (Class I, June 2026, 196 units): sheath leakage not visible on inspection.

Caveats. Injury and death counts are manufacturer reports to FDA and will be revised; causality is not adjudicated.

For us. 'Purge Pressure Low' or a cassette-not-recognized alarm is not a nuisance. Have a second controller available for transports and OR cases, and know which cassette generation your hospital stocks.

item.title: Multicentre RCT: caudal block does not increase fistula after hypospadias repair and gives better analgesia
item.description:
Reg Anesth Pain Med · RCT · 2026-09-11

210 children under 2 years having primary distal or midshaft hypospadias repair at 16 Pediatric Regional Anesthesia Network centres were randomised to caudal or penile block. Urethrocutaneous fistula at 3 months was 8.9% vs 7.3%.

Take-home

  • Fistula 8.9% caudal vs 7.3% penile (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.35-2.76); proximal meatus was the real risk factor (RR 2.8).
  • Caudal: fewer received intraoperative opioid (33% vs 56%) or rescue opioid (4.9% vs 15.7%); lower PACU pain scores.
  • Stopped early with 77% follow-up, so wide CIs; still the best evidence yet against the caudal-fistula hypothesis.

Why it matters. For a decade paediatric anaesthesiologists and urologists have argued over retrospective reports linking caudal block to urethrocutaneous fistula after hypospadias repair, and many centres switched to penile blocks on that basis. This is the randomised answer from the Pediatric Regional Anesthesia Network.

What they did. Multicentre non-inferiority RCT at 16 PRAN centres (NCT02861950). Children under 2 years having primary midshaft or distal hypospadias repair were randomised to caudal block or penile block, both under general anaesthesia. Primary outcome: urethrocutaneous fistula within 3 months.

What they found.

  • 210 randomised; 161 (76.6%) completed 3-month follow-up (79 caudal, 82 penile).
  • Fistula 7/79 (8.9%) caudal vs 6/82 (7.3%) penile; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.35-2.76, p=0.9.
  • Proximal meatal position was the real predictor: RR 2.8, 95% CI 1.48-5.30, p=0.002.
  • Caudal group: fewer received intraoperative opioid (33% vs 56%, p<0.001) or rescue opioid (4.9% vs 15.7%, p=0.01), and PACU FLACC scores were lower (0.49 vs 1.14, p=0.03).

Caveats. The trial ended early with incomplete enrolment and a quarter lost to follow-up, so the confidence interval is wide and a clinically relevant difference cannot be excluded. The authors call the findings exploratory.

What it means. The best available evidence does not support abandoning caudals for distal hypospadias: the block gives better analgesia and the fistula risk tracks the anatomy, not the needle. A reasonable basis to bring the caudal back where it was dropped on retrospective data.

item.title: Class I recall widens for Medline-reprocessed AcuNav, ViewFlex and SoundStar ICE catheters over residual particulates
item.description:
FDA · Safety alert · 2026-09-02

FDA's most serious recall classification, first assigned in March 2026 and expanded in June and September, covers reprocessed intracardiac echo and electrophysiology catheters that may carry particulate matter on patient-contacting surfaces.

Take-home

  • Affected: Medline ReNewal reprocessed ACUSON AcuNav 8F and 10F, St. Jude ViewFlex and Biosense Webster SoundStar ultrasound catheters.
  • Risk: inflammation, infection, granuloma or thrombus with cerebral or pulmonary embolism; no injuries reported as of May 18.
  • Check lot numbers against FDA's list; quarantine, then return or destroy per Medline's instructions.

Why it matters. ICE is now standard imaging for left atrial appendage occlusion, transseptal work and many EP ablations, and reprocessed single-use catheters are common for cost reasons. A particulate problem in a catheter that sits in the right atrium for hours is everyone's problem in the room.

What happened. Medline Industries recalled specific lots of its ReNewal reprocessed catheters because they may contain small residual particulates. FDA classified the recall as Class I, the most serious category, on March 5, 2026; affected lots were added on June 18 and again on September 2, 2026, with the FDA early-alert page updated September 3. The ultrasound catheters named are the St. Jude ViewFlex, Biosense Webster SoundStar, and ACUSON AcuNav 8F and 10F. Also included are St. Jude Livewire, Response and Supreme diagnostic catheters, the Abbott Inquiry and the Biosense Webster CS catheter.

The risk. FDA states that particulates on patient-contacting surfaces could cause an inflammatory response or systemic infection, and that if they dislodge into blood or the heart they could cause a granulomatous reaction or thrombus leading to cerebral or pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis. As of May 18, Medline had reported no serious injuries or deaths linked to the issue.

What to do. Quarantine affected stock, complete Medline's response form, and destroy affected product after recall actions are complete; lots from the earlier notice should be returned instead. Medline sent customer letters on December 22 and May 15.

For us. If your structural or EP lab uses reprocessed ICE catheters, ask today whether the lots have been checked against FDA's list. Unexplained fever or an embolic event after an ICE-guided case now has one more item on the differential.

item.title: AHA: residual lesions drive unplanned reintervention in ~5% of pediatric heart operations; catch them in the OR
item.description:
Circulation · Consensus · 2026-09-01

AHA scientific statement on important residual lesions and early unplanned reinterventions after pediatric cardiac surgery: incidence, risk factors, monitoring, imaging, catheterization and reoperation, and family communication.

Take-home

  • Unplanned same-admission reintervention follows about 5% of pediatric cardiac operations, more in infants and complex repairs.
  • Linked to higher mortality, morbidity and resource use, with wide center variation in how fast it happens.
  • Institutional backing for a systematic post-bypass TEE check and early catheterization when recovery stalls.

Why it matters. After the surgeon closes, the single biggest determinant of a child's course is whether a hemodynamically important residual lesion was left behind. Unplanned reintervention during the same admission happens in roughly 5% of pediatric cardiac operations and carries higher mortality, morbidity and cost, with wide center-to-center variation in how quickly it happens.

What it is. An American Heart Association scientific statement (Circulation 2026;154:e573-e588), first author John Costello, with Jane Newburger and Meena Nathan among the writing group, published 1 September 2026.

What it says.

  • Good outcomes depend on a complete anatomic and physiologic diagnosis, a sound operative plan, a technically complete repair supported by lesion-specific anesthetic and perfusion strategies, and expert postoperative care.
  • Residual lesions and early unplanned reinterventions are more common in younger patients and more complex operations.
  • It reviews the postoperative monitoring patterns and clinical signs that should raise suspicion, the noninvasive imaging used to identify and quantify residual lesions, the role of diagnostic and interventional catheterization, and surgical considerations for reoperation.
  • It stresses clear communication with families and lays out research priorities.

Caveats. A consensus synthesis rather than new data; it does not prescribe a single imaging algorithm or a timing rule for reintervention.

For the anesthesiologist. The person best placed to catch a residual VSD, outflow gradient or valve leak before the chest is closed is the one holding the TEE probe. This statement is institutional backing for a systematic post-bypass TEE checklist, for speaking up when the image does not match the plan, and for early catheterization rather than days of watching a child who is not progressing.

item.title: iHOPE: spinal vs general anaesthesia for hip fracture makes no difference to death or cardiopulmonary complications
item.description:
Lancet Healthy Longevity · RCT · 2026-09-01

771 patients aged 65 or older at 22 German hospitals were randomised to spinal or general anaesthesia for hip fracture surgery. The 30-day composite of death and new serious cardiac or pulmonary complications was 14% vs 12%.

Take-home

  • Composite death/serious cardiopulmonary complications: 14% spinal vs 12% general (adjusted HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.83-1.82).
  • Trial stopped at 75% of target (slow recruitment, COVID-19); crossover was substantial, so interpret cautiously.
  • Third large RCT after REGAIN and RAGA with the same answer: pick the technique that fits the patient.

Why it matters. REGAIN (NEJM 2021) and RAGA (JAMA 2022) found no difference between spinal and general anaesthesia for hip fracture in North America and China. iHOPE is the European pragmatic trial that many expected to show a benefit of spinal on hard cardiopulmonary outcomes.

What they did. Open-label, pragmatic RCT at 22 German hospitals (April 2018 to February 2023). Patients aged 65 or older having hip fracture surgery were randomised 1:1, stratified by centre, to spinal or general anaesthesia. Primary outcome: time to a composite of all-cause death and new serious cardiac or pulmonary complications within 30 days. Registered DRKS00013644; funded by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research.

What they found (771 analysed; 69% women).

  • Primary endpoint 55/385 (14%) spinal vs 47/386 (12%) general; adjusted HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.83-1.82, p=0.29.
  • Mean time to the composite 10.2 vs 10.5 days.
  • Adverse events 83% vs 89%; serious adverse events 34% vs 31%; no treatment-related deaths.

Caveats. Stopped early at 75% of the target sample because of slow recruitment and COVID-19 staffing shortages, so power is modest; crossover between arms was high. The authors themselves urge caution and conclude that there is no clinically meaningful difference. Delirium and functional recovery were not the primary question.

What it means. Three large trials on three continents now agree: the anaesthetic technique does not move mortality or major complications after hip fracture. The decision belongs to the individual patient (anticoagulation, cognition, cardiac status, preference) and to doing either technique well, with good blocks and blood pressure control.

item.title: LAACS-2: routine surgical appendage closure did not cut stroke overall; benefit signal only in high-risk patients
item.description:
ESC Congress 2026 (Hot Line) · Conference · 2026-08-31

Randomized trial of 1,500 patients having first-time elective cardiac surgery in Denmark, Spain and Sweden, with or without concomitant left atrial appendage closure regardless of atrial fibrillation history, presented as a Hot Line at ESC 2026.

Take-home

  • Stroke or TIA over median 4 years: 4.28% with closure vs 5.04% without, HR 0.85, P=0.52.
  • In patients with CHA2DS2-VASc above the median, closure was associated with a 56% reduction (P=0.018).
  • Only 4% had prior AF; LAAOS III remains the evidence for patients who already have AF.

Why it matters. LAAOS III proved appendage occlusion prevents stroke in surgical patients with pre-existing AF. The next question was whether every sternotomy should include an AtriClip to pre-empt future AF-related stroke. LAACS-2 tested exactly that.

What they did. Helena Dominguez presented the trial at ESC Congress 2026 on 31 August. At four centers in Denmark, Spain and Sweden, 1,500 patients undergoing first-time elective cardiac surgery (about 60% CABG, 30% aortic, 8% mitral; mean age 67; only 4.1% with prior AF) were randomized 1:1 to concomitant LAA closure, AtriClip encouraged, or no closure. Follow-up used national registries with blinded neurologist adjudication; median follow-up 4.0 years. Of 747 assigned to closure, 676 received it.

What they found.

  • Primary endpoint, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke or TIA: 32 vs 38 events, 4.28% vs 5.04%, HR 0.85 (95% CI 0.53-1.37), P=0.517.
  • Patients with baseline CHA2DS2-VASc above the median: 56% relative reduction (P=0.018); no benefit in lower-risk patients.
  • No difference in mortality.

Caveats. Low event rate and wide confidence interval; crossover and non-adherence; a CABG-heavy population with little AF, so it says nothing against closure in patients with AF; the subgroup is hypothesis-generating; no publication identified at the time of the congress; complications of the clip were not yet reported.

For the anesthesiologist. Routine appendage closure in everyone is not supported, so expect surgeons to target it to higher CHA2DS2-VASc patients and to anyone with AF. On TEE, keep documenting the appendage before and after clip placement; residual stumps and incomplete exclusion are the failure mode.

item.title: TRIC-I-HF: transcatheter tricuspid repair cut death or heart failure hospitalization by 60% over 3 years
item.description:
NEJM · RCT · 2026-08-30

German randomized trial of 360 patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation and high heart failure risk, comparing transcatheter tricuspid repair plus medical therapy with medical therapy alone, published in NEJM and presented at ESC 2026.

Take-home

  • One-year hierarchical endpoint (death, HF hospitalization, quality of life): win ratio 2.42.
  • Freedom from death or HF hospitalization at 3 years 52.4% vs 21.0%, HR 0.40; NNT about 4 at 1 year.
  • 98% had edge-to-edge repair; 30-day major adverse events 5.9%, mortality 0.4%.

Why it matters. TRILUMINATE and TRISCEND II showed tricuspid transcatheter therapy improves symptoms and quality of life but not survival. TRIC-I-HF is the first randomized trial to show fewer deaths and admissions, which is what has been missing from the argument for treating the 'forgotten valve'.

What they did. Jörg Hausleiter and Thomas Stocker led an open-label trial at 29 German heart valve centers. 360 patients (mean age 80, 56% women) with symptomatic severe or greater TR and increased risk of heart failure events were randomized 2:1 to transcatheter tricuspid repair plus optimal medical therapy (n=237) or medical therapy alone (n=123). 98% of interventions were edge-to-edge repair (TriClip or PASCAL); a few had annuloplasty or replacement.

What they found.

  • One-year hierarchical composite of death, HF hospitalization and failure to improve KCCQ by 15 points: win ratio 2.42 (95% CI 1.76-3.33), P<0.001.
  • Freedom from death or HF hospitalization at 3 years: 52.4% vs 21.0%, HR 0.40 (0.29-0.55), with both components reduced.
  • 30-day safety: major adverse events 5.9%, major bleeding 2.5%, mortality 0.4%.

Caveats. Open label; a selected, high-risk, very elderly population treated at expert centers; the control arm event rate was very high. Published simultaneously in NEJM (doi 10.1056/NEJMoa2606934).

For the anesthesiologist. Tricuspid TEER volumes will rise, and the procedure lives or dies on TEE imaging of the septal-anterior coaptation gap, often with deep transgastric and 3D views, under general anesthesia. Isolated surgical tricuspid repair remains the comparator nobody has randomized.

item.title: TAVI PCI: doing the valve first and the stent later was noninferior to PCI before TAVI in severe AS with CAD
item.description:
NEJM · RCT · 2026-08-30

Randomized trial of 986 patients with severe aortic stenosis and significant coronary disease comparing TAVI-first with PCI-first sequencing, presented at ESC 2026 and published in NEJM.

Take-home

  • One-year composite 22.2% TAVI-first vs 24.2% PCI-first; noninferiority met, no subgroup heterogeneity.
  • Fewer patients in the TAVI-first arm ended up needing PCI at all; bleeding tended higher with PCI first.
  • Combined with PRO-TAVI, routine pre-TAVI PCI is losing its rationale.

Why it matters. Half of TAVI candidates have coronary disease, and the reflex has been to stent first so the heart tolerates rapid pacing and valve deployment. That reflex costs antiplatelet exposure and bleeding in 82-year-olds.

What they did. Barbara Stähli presented the trial at ESC Congress 2026 in Munich on 30 August, with simultaneous NEJM publication (doi 10.1056/NEJMoa2606924). 986 patients with severe AS and concomitant significant CAD were randomized to TAVI followed by PCI or PCI followed by TAVI, with the second procedure within about 45 days (median 27 days TAVI-first, 13 days PCI-first).

What they found.

  • Primary one-year composite of death, nonfatal MI, ischemia-driven revascularization, major or worse bleeding, and valve-, procedure- or heart-failure-related rehospitalization: 22.2% vs 24.2%, meeting noninferiority.
  • No significant differences in individual components; major bleeding tended to be more frequent with PCI first.
  • Fewer TAVI-first patients ultimately underwent PCI, because lesions were reassessed after the valve was in.
  • No heterogeneity by age, sex or PCI complexity.

Caveats. Noninferiority design; the window between procedures was short, so this does not test indefinite deferral; exclusion criteria were not detailed in the congress coverage. PRO-TAVI (ACC.26, Lancet) separately showed that deferring PCI altogether was noninferior with less bleeding.

For the anesthesiologist. Expect more TAVI patients arriving with untreated proximal lesions. Rapid pacing and hypotension during deployment in the presence of a tight LAD is the moment to be ready, and the hemodynamic plan should be discussed with the interventionalist beforehand.

item.title: Routine protamine after transfemoral TAVI reduced death or bleeding at 30 days, at the price of more anaphylaxis
item.description:
ESC Congress 2026 (Hot Line) · Conference · 2026-08-30

Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial of routine versus selective protamine before large-bore sheath removal in 966 transfemoral TAVI patients, presented as a Hot Line at ESC Congress 2026.

Take-home

  • Primary composite of death or clinically relevant (VARC-3 type 1-4) bleeding at 30 days was reduced with routine protamine.
  • The benefit came from less clinically relevant bleeding; major bleeding and hard outcomes were not clearly improved.
  • Anaphylaxis was more frequent with routine protamine (P=0.01), without anaphylaxis deaths; no excess thromboembolism.

Why it matters. Whether to reverse heparin after TAVI has been decided by habit: many centers give protamine routinely, others only for ooze. Both camps worried about the other's complication, bleeding versus thrombosis or anaphylaxis. This is the first double-blind trial to settle it.

What they did. Christiaan Overduin presented POPular ACE TAVI in Hot Line 7 at ESC Congress 2026 in Munich (30 August 2026). An investigator-initiated, multicenter, double-blind trial randomized transfemoral TAVI patients to routine protamine or placebo (selective protamine) before removal of the large-bore arterial sheath; 966 patients formed the final population. The primary endpoint was all-cause death or clinically relevant bleeding (VARC-3 type 1-4) at 30 days.

What they found.

  • Routine protamine significantly reduced the primary composite, driven by less clinically relevant bleeding at 30 days.
  • Anaphylaxis was more frequent with routine protamine (P=0.01), with no anaphylaxis-related deaths.
  • There was no increase in thromboembolic events.

Caveats. Event rates and effect sizes were not released in the congress coverage, and no simultaneous publication has appeared; the discussant noted the trial does not show prevention of major bleeding or improvement in hard outcomes, and that optimal heparin dose and target ACT during TAVI remain unsettled.

For the anesthesiologist. Protamine is our drug. If your TAVI program moves to routine reversal, the anaphylaxis signal means the anesthesia team, not just the operator, should be present and ready for sheath removal, with the usual caution in patients with prior protamine exposure, NPH insulin use or fish allergy. Ask for the full paper before changing protocol.

item.title: 2026 ESC HF guideline: HFmrEF is gone, shock teams Class I, no routine ECMO or IABP in AMI shock, LVAD Class I
item.description:
Eur Heart J · Guideline · 2026-08-28

Full revision of the ESC heart failure guideline, endorsed by EACTS, published online in European Heart Journal on 28 August 2026 and presented at ESC Congress in Munich.

Take-home

  • Two phenotypes only: HFrEF (LVEF below 50%) and HFpEF (50% or more); 'acute' heart failure becomes 'decompensated'.
  • Shock team to guide temporary MCS is Class I; microaxial pump IIa in selected STEMI shock; tMCS and IABP Class III in unselected AMI shock.
  • Durable LVAD strengthened to Class I in selected patients; M-TEER upgraded; continuous inotropes as a bridge move up to IIa.

Why it matters. The ESC heart failure guideline is the European reference and this is the first full rewrite since 2021 (chairs Kober and Adamo; Eur Heart J, online 28 August 2026 at ESC Congress in Munich).

Big-picture changes. HFmrEF is gone; HFrEF now means LVEF below 50% and HFpEF 50% or above. 'Acute' becomes 'decompensated'. Stages A to D are adopted.

Cardiogenic shock and temporary MCS.

  • A multidisciplinary Shock Team to guide device selection is Class I.
  • A microaxial flow pump should be considered (IIa) in selected STEMI-related shock with LV dysfunction and no risk of hypoxic brain injury.
  • Temporary MCS is not recommended (Class III, harm) in unselected AMI shock, and IABP is not recommended (Class III) in unselected cardiogenic shock.
  • Temporary MCS should be considered (IIa) as a bridge for mechanical complications of MI, and for HF-related instability as bridge to recovery, decision, candidacy or transplant.
  • Continuous inotropes move from IIb to IIa as a bridge in advanced HFrEF with low output and hypoperfusion.

Advanced HF and durable support.

  • Early referral to an advanced HF centre for motivated patients without absolute contraindications is Class I.
  • The durable LVAD recommendation is strengthened to Class I for selected patients, reported as an upgrade from IIa that aligns with US guidance; cardiac rehabilitation after LVAD is Class I.
  • Proactive goals-of-care discussions and integrated palliative care in advanced HF are Class I.

Caveats. European practice, and several shock recommendations rest on single trials (DanGer Shock, ECLS-SHOCK).

For us. The shock-team mandate, the explicit 'no routine ECMO or balloon' stance and inotropes as an accepted bridge set what colleagues will expect at the bedside, and they line up with the EACTS/STS/AATS surgical guideline from last October.

item.title: Fifth Universal Definition of MI drops types 1-5; CABG and PCI infarcts become 'procedure-related MI'
item.description:
Eur Heart J · Consensus · 2026-08-28

ESC, ACC, AHA and World Heart Federation consensus released at ESC Congress 2026 (European Heart Journal), replacing the numbered MI types with primary, secondary and procedure-related categories.

Take-home

  • Three categories: primary (plaque event), secondary (supply-demand), procedure-related (within 30 days of a cardiac procedure).
  • Sex-specific troponin 99th percentile limits are called for; coding aligns with ICD-11.
  • Expect trial endpoints and quality metrics for CABG-related MI to be redefined over the next year.

Why it matters. Every cardiac surgery trial, registry and quality program counts perioperative MI, and type 5 MI (after CABG) has been one of the most contested definitions in cardiology, with surgical and interventional groups favoring different thresholds. The new document changes the framework rather than just the cutoffs.

What it says. Released 28 August 2026 ahead of its ESC Congress presentation, the Fifth Universal Definition is a joint ESC, ACC, AHA and WHF statement published in European Heart Journal (doi 10.1093/eurheartj/ehag101).

  • The numbered types 1 to 5 are replaced by three clinical settings: primary MI (a spontaneous acute coronary event such as plaque rupture, dissection, spasm or thrombus), secondary MI (oxygen supply-demand imbalance from another condition), and procedure-related MI, defined as occurring within 30 days of a cardiac procedure such as PCI or CABG.
  • It calls for sex-specific 99th percentile troponin thresholds.
  • Categories map to ICD-11 codes to support surveillance.

Caveats. The press release does not spell out the biomarker thresholds for procedure-related MI after CABG, and that detail will decide how disruptive this is for surgical trials; read the full text before changing local definitions.

For the anesthesiologist. Your institution's M&M, your STS data manager and every ongoing cardiac surgery trial will have to re-map endpoints. When a colleague says 'type 2 MI' or 'type 5 MI' at the ICU handoff, that language is now officially obsolete; secondary MI and procedure-related MI are the terms.

item.title: Cold-stored platelets kept up to 21 days are noninferior to room-temperature platelets for surgical bleeding (CHIPS)
item.description:
JAMA · RCT · 2026-08-17

Phase 3 adaptive noninferiority RCT at 27 US and Australian sites: 989 bleeding cardiac surgical patients randomized 2:1 to cold-stored platelets (up to 21 days) or room-temperature platelets (up to 7 days).

Take-home

  • Cold-stored platelets up to 21 days were noninferior to room-temperature platelets for active surgical bleeding.
  • Chest tube output, thrombosis and mortality similar; reexploration slightly higher with cold platelets.
  • Expect 21-day cold platelets in trauma bays and smaller hospitals that could never stock platelets.

Why it matters. Room-temperature platelets expire at 5-7 days and are chronically short, which is why many trauma centres cannot stock them and why the military and some civilian programs have used cold-stored platelets under FDA variance. CHIPS is the trial that tests whether cold storage, out to 21 days, costs hemostatic efficacy.

What they did. Phase 3, 27-site (US and Australia), 2:1 randomized, partially blinded, adaptive noninferiority trial with storage-duration ranging, December 2021 to March 2025. Cardiac surgical patients with active bleeding needing platelets got cold-stored platelets (up to 21 days) or room-temperature platelets (up to 7 days). 1,000 were transfused; 989 analyzed (650 vs 339).

What they found.

  • Primary hemostatic efficacy score (1-5, higher means more bleeding; margin 1 point): noninferior at every storage duration, posterior probability above 99.9%; pooled mean difference 0.09 (95% credible interval -0.06 to 0.23).
  • 24-h chest tube output 8.9 vs 8.4 mL/kg (difference 0.4, 95% CI -1.0 to 1.5).
  • Thrombotic events, transfusion reactions, ARDS, renal failure, septic shock and mortality similar. Reexploration was more frequent in the cold-stored arm, the one exception worth watching.

Caveats. Cardiac surgery, not trauma; a Bayesian efficacy score rather than a hard clinical endpoint; partially blinded.

For the anesthesiologist. This is the evidence base that lets blood banks carry 21-day cold platelets for bleeding patients, which matters most for trauma bays, smaller hospitals and prehospital programs. It sits alongside the negative CLIP-II result for cryopreserved platelets published eight months earlier: cold storage works, deep-freezing did not.

item.title: NRP beats direct procurement for early survival after DCD heart transplant; curves merge after the first month
item.description:
JTCVS · Registry · 2026-08-13

A propensity-matched UNOS analysis of 2,831 US DCD heart transplants (2019 to March 2026) found a modest early survival advantage with normothermic regional perfusion over direct procurement that disappears among one-month survivors.

Take-home

  • DCD is now 24.6% of US adult heart transplants; 61% recovered by direct procurement, 39% by NRP.
  • Survival NRP versus DPP: 97.9% versus 95.8% at 1 month, 86.9% versus 83.5% at 3 years.
  • Among patients alive at 1 month, outcomes were identical; the NRP benefit is perioperative.

Why it matters. DCD hearts are now about a quarter of US adult heart transplants, recovered either by direct procurement with ex situ machine perfusion (DPP) or by thoraco-abdominal NRP. Whether NRP gives better grafts is a live argument, now entangled with the ethical scrutiny of NRP itself. This is the largest national comparison (Shou and colleagues, Stanford; J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg, online 13 August 2026).

What they did. UNOS registry analysis of 2,831 first-time adult isolated DCD heart transplants from January 2019 to March 2026, during which DCD made up 24.6% of adult heart transplants. DPP was defined as death-to-cross-clamp of 30 minutes or less, NRP as longer. 939 propensity-matched pairs were compared.

What they found.

  • Survival at 1 month: 97.9% with NRP versus 95.8% with DPP (P = 0.01).
  • 1 year: 92% versus 90% (P = 0.05); 3 years: 86.9% versus 83.5% (P = 0.04).
  • Among patients alive at 1 month, 1-year survival was identical at 94.0%, and among those alive at 1 year, 3-year survival did not differ.
  • Conclusion: NRP carries a modest perioperative survival advantage; after the first month the curves run together.

Caveats. Observational, procurement method inferred from timing rather than recorded, no data on early graft dysfunction grade, MCS use or center experience, and NRP centers may differ systematically from DPP centers.

For us. The NRP advantage is an early one, which fits less ischemic injury and less early graft dysfunction. Expect DPP hearts to need more support in the first hours, and expect this paper to be quoted in the NRP policy debate.

item.title: AHA statement gives pediatric cardiogenic shock a definition, severity stages and an escalation framework
item.description:
Circulation · Consensus · 2026-08-06

AHA scientific statement on heart-failure-related cardiogenic shock in children: bedside diagnostic framework, proposed definition and staging aligned with validated systems, stabilisation, monitoring and timing of mechanical support.

Take-home

  • Proposes a shared definition and severity staging so a child's trajectory reads the same in every unit.
  • Many children keep deteriorating through the first 24 hours; timely escalation to MCS is central.
  • Use the staging language to argue for planned cannulation before a crash ECPR.

Why it matters. Pediatric cardiogenic shock has had no agreed definition, no severity staging and no standard escalation pathway, unlike adult shock where SCAI staging reshaped team behavior. Children with myocarditis, cardiomyopathy or failing single-ventricle circulations often deteriorate for a day before anyone calls the ECMO or VAD team.

What it is. An American Heart Association scientific statement (Circulation 2026;154:e374-e392) from a writing group led by Kriti Puri with pediatric cardiology, critical care, heart failure and surgical representation.

What it says.

  • Heart-failure-related cardiogenic shock in children carries high morbidity and mortality and has been poorly studied.
  • It proposes a working definition and a severity staging aligned with previously validated systems, so that a child's trajectory can be described consistently across units.
  • It offers a bedside diagnostic framework, initial stabilization steps for suspected shock, and a review of noninvasive and invasive monitoring to judge whether a child is improving or sliding.
  • It stresses that many children continue to deteriorate during the first 24 hours and that timely decisions about escalation to mechanical circulatory support are central to survival.
  • Research priorities include frontline education, the multidisciplinary team, biomarkers and decision tools for individualised care.

Caveats. A consensus framework rather than a validated score; the staging needs prospective validation in pediatric cohorts, and device selection specifics are left to local programs.

For the anesthesiologist. You meet these children at the worst moments: induction for ECMO cannulation, VAD implant or transplant, or a diagnostic cath in a child in compensated shock. A shared staging language gives you a defensible way to say this child needs support before the next anaesthetic, and to push for earlier, planned cannulation rather than a crash ECPR.

item.title: ICECAP: longer cooling at 33 C after out-of-hospital arrest does not improve neurological outcome; 6 h matched 48 h
item.description:
JAMA · RCT · 2026-08-05

A 71-hospital US adaptive trial randomized 1,158 comatose survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, all cooled to 33 C, to durations from 6 to 72 hours.

Take-home

  • No duration-response: outcomes with 6 or 12 hours matched 18-48 hours in shockable and nonshockable cohorts.
  • Posterior probability that 6 hours was the shortest optimal duration about 0.51; trial stopped early.
  • If you cool to 33 C, there is no reason to hold it 24-48 hours; fever control still matters.

Why it matters. Even after TTM2, many centers still cool selected patients to 33 C, and the usual 24 hours is a convention, not a tested dose. ICECAP (Influence of Cooling duration on Efficacy in Cardiac Arrest Patients), funded by NIH through the SIREN network and published in JAMA online 5 August 2026, is the first randomized duration-finding trial.

What they did. Meurer, Yeatts, Geocadin and colleagues enrolled 1,158 comatose adults after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (883 nonshockable, 275 shockable) at 71 US hospitals from 2020 to 2025. All were cooled to 33 C with closed-loop devices; the first 200 were randomized to 12, 24 or 48 hours, then a Bayesian response-adaptive algorithm allocated patients across 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42 and 48 hours (60- and 72-hour arms were never opened). The primary outcome was a weighted modified Rankin Scale at 90 days with blinded central assessment, analyzed as a duration-response curve.

What they found. There was no duration-response in either cohort. In nonshockable patients, the posterior probability that 6 hours was the shortest duration achieving the maximal outcome was 0.51 (0.31 for 12 hours, 0.01-0.07 for each longer arm); shockable patients were similar (0.49 for 6 hours). Raw 90-day mortality in nonshockable patients ranged from 77.5% to 88.8% across arms with no trend. The trial stopped at an interim analysis after a prespecified rule favoring the shortest duration was met.

Caveats. No normothermia control, so this says nothing about whether cooling helps at all. Shockable-rhythm numbers were small. Clinicians and families knew the allocated duration.

For anesthesiologists. Combined with TTM2 and the 2025 AHA range of 32-37.5 C, this removes the rationale for prolonged 33 C cooling. Controlled rewarming and active fever prevention for 36 hours or more remain the parts of temperature control with support.

item.title: Video laryngoscopy beats direct for routine OR intubation: first-pass 88% hyperangulated vs 78% direct (COVALENT)
item.description:
JAMA Netw Open · RCT · 2026-08-03

Three-arm RCT of 2,423 elective surgical patients at six centres in Germany and Austria comparing direct laryngoscopy, video laryngoscopy with a Macintosh blade, and video laryngoscopy with a hyperangulated blade.

Take-home

  • First-pass success 78% direct, 83% video Macintosh, 88% video hyperangulated in 2,423 elective intubations.
  • Fewer rescue mask ventilations and operator switches with video; no more trauma to teeth or lips.
  • Hyperangulated video blade is the logical default under in-line stabilization.

Why it matters. Video laryngoscopy has won in the ED and ICU, but routine OR intubation still largely runs on direct laryngoscopy. COVALENT is the largest OR trial, and it separates standard-blade from hyperangulated video devices.

What they did. Three-arm RCT at six centres in Germany and Austria (March 2022 to February 2025). Adults needing intubation for elective surgery were randomized 1:1:1 to direct laryngoscopy, video laryngoscopy with a Macintosh blade, or video laryngoscopy with a hyperangulated blade, stratified by site and Mallampati class. 2,532 randomized; 2,423 analyzed. Several device brands were used.

What they found.

  • First-pass success: 78.2% direct, 82.9% video Macintosh, 87.6% video hyperangulated; every pairwise comparison P<.001.
  • Cormack-Lehane grade 1 views: 58.8%, 74.7%, 87.6%.
  • Intermittent mask ventilation needed in 11.8% with direct vs about 4% with either video device; fewer operator switches with video.
  • Time to glottic view shortest with hyperangulated (14.1 s vs 16.7 vs 20.5), yet time to capnography was about 72 s in all arms.
  • No difference in desaturation, regurgitation or dental injury overall; after a failed first attempt, lip or dental injury or blood on the blade was lower with the hyperangulated blade (10.9% vs about 23-24%).

Caveats. Operators unblinded; elective patients; the outcome is first-pass success, not patient harm; JAMA Network Open rather than a flagship journal.

For the anesthesiologist. The authors call video laryngoscopy the new standard for routine airway management. For trauma it strengthens the case for a hyperangulated video blade as first choice under manual in-line stabilization, where the view, not the time, is the limiting factor.

item.title: Four doses of dapagliflozin around cardiac surgery nearly halve postoperative AKI
item.description:
JAMA · RCT · 2026-07-30

A Dutch double-blind trial in 7 hospitals randomized 784 elective cardiac surgery patients to dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo from the day before surgery through postoperative day 2.

Take-home

  • AKI within 7 days: 28% vs 52%; RR 0.54 (95% CI 0.45-0.65).
  • No excess atrial fibrillation (45% both) or reoperation (11% vs 10%).
  • Cheap, short, and already on formulary; watch for ketoacidosis and confirm in other cohorts.

Why it matters. Cardiac surgery-associated AKI affects roughly a third of patients and nothing pharmacological has reliably prevented it. SGLT2 inhibitors protect kidneys in chronic disease, and this trial (Oosterom-Eijmael and colleagues, JAMA online 30 July 2026) is the first adequately powered perioperative test.

What they did. 784 adults undergoing elective cardiac surgery at 2 academic and 5 non-academic Dutch hospitals were randomized, double-blind, to dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo once daily, starting the day before surgery and continuing through postoperative day 2 (four doses). The primary outcome was AKI by KDIGO criteria within 7 postoperative days.

What they found. AKI occurred in 28% of the dapagliflozin group vs 52% of the placebo group (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.45-0.65; P less than .001). Postoperative atrial fibrillation was 45% in both arms and reoperation 11% vs 10%. The published abstract does not report dialysis, mortality or ketoacidosis rates in detail, so those need the full paper.

Caveats. The placebo-arm AKI rate of 52% is high, which suggests sensitive creatinine-based ascertainment and amplifies the absolute difference. Most of the benefit will be stage 1 AKI unless the full results show otherwise. Euglycemic ketoacidosis with perioperative SGLT2 inhibitors is a known concern and the usual advice is to stop them 3-4 days before surgery, which this trial deliberately contradicted; safety data on ketoacidosis will decide uptake.

For anesthesiologists. This is the most promising renoprotective drug result in cardiac surgery in years and it is actionable at the preoperative visit. Expect protocol discussions with surgeons and nephrologists; the sensible position is to await the full safety data and confirmatory trials before routine adoption, while no longer reflexively stopping SGLT2 inhibitors in patients already taking them.

item.title: FDA licenses Ezplaz, the first US freeze-dried plasma: room-temperature storage, reconstituted in minutes
item.description:
FDA · FDA/Regulatory · 2026-07-29

On July 29, 2026 the FDA granted a biologics license to Vascular Solutions (Teleflex) for Ezplaz, a single-donor freeze-dried plasma for adults who need plasma when other plasma products are unavailable.

Take-home

  • First FDA-licensed freeze-dried plasma: stored 2-25 C for 12 months, reconstituted in about 1-2.5 minutes.
  • Label: adults needing plasma when other plasma products are unavailable, including massive transfusion and warfarin bleeding.
  • A logistics win; no trial shows Ezplaz itself improves survival.

Why it matters. The US has run military dried plasma on emergency use authorizations for a decade while France, Germany and others used it routinely. On July 29, 2026 the FDA issued a biologics license for Ezplaz (Vascular Solutions LLC, a Teleflex subsidiary), the first freeze-dried plasma approved for US use.

What it is. A single unit of fresh frozen plasma, freeze-dried into a plastic bag rather than glass, from male-only donors to limit TRALI, supplied as group AB or group A with low-titer anti-B. Stored at 2-25 C for up to 12 months, reconstituted with the supplied sterile water in about 1-2.5 minutes, and given IV or IO. The kit includes the transfer and transfusion sets.

Label. Adults who need plasma when other plasma products are not available: bleeding or pre-procedure patients with multiple factor deficiencies, massive transfusion with clinically significant coagulopathy, and bleeding warfarin patients. Contraindications are plasma hypersensitivity and IgA deficiency. Labeling notes limited effect on minimally elevated INR (about 1.5-1.7). A postmarketing safety study focused on thrombotic events has been reported as a condition of approval.

Caveats. This is a logistics approval, not an outcome claim. Prehospital plasma RCTs were mixed (PAMPer positive in air transport, COMBAT and the French lyophilized-plasma trial neutral), and no trial has shown Ezplaz itself changes mortality. The Defense Health Agency has prioritized a licensed domestic source, so military demand will shape early supply.

For the anesthesiologist. Expect dried plasma in rural EDs, helicopters, hybrid ORs and mass-casualty caches, and in the first bags that arrive with transferred patients. The Joint Trauma System issued a companion CPG on June 9, 2026 covering dried plasma use across roles of care, including as a 1:1 partner for red cells when whole blood is unavailable.
